How to Test a Diode with a Digital Multimeter: Diode Mode, Resistance Mode, Expected Readings and Fault Diagnosis

A diode is one of the easiest parts to check on the bench, but a wrong meter setting or an in circuit reading still catches many technicians out. Below we cover diode mode, resistance mode, the readings to expect from each diode family and a simple current calculator.

Diode Mode Forward Voltage Table Open and Short Faults In Circuit Testing Vf Calculator

The multimeter steps, the forward voltage each diode family should show and how to spot open, shorted and leaky parts, plus a free calculator for series resistor current.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how to test a diode with a digital multimeter, read the numbers correctly and decide in seconds whether the part is good or bad.
Quick Answer

How to test a diode with a digital multimeter?

How to test a diode: switch off power, set the multimeter to diode mode, place the red probe on the anode and the black probe on the cathode, then reverse the probes. A good silicon diode reads about 0.5 to 0.8 V forward and OL in reverse. For example, a healthy 1N4007 typically shows around 0.6 V one way and OL the other way.

  1. Switch off power and discharge nearby capacitors
  2. Set the multimeter to the diode symbol
  3. Red probe on anode, black probe on cathode and note the reading
  4. Swap the probes and note the reverse reading
  5. Good diode: about 0.5 to 0.8 V forward and OL in reverse

What Is Diode Testing?

Diode testing means checking that a diode conducts in one direction and blocks in the other, and every bench technician should know how to test a diode. A healthy part shows a small forward voltage drop with the probes one way and an open reading with the probes reversed.

Key Facts
  • Fluke states that a good silicon diode shows about 0.5 to 0.8 V in diode test mode
  • Germanium diodes read lower, roughly 0.2 to 0.3 V according to Fluke
  • A good diode shows OL when reverse biased
  • OL in both directions means open, a low reading both ways means shorted

A diode is a PN junction that lets current flow from anode to cathode once the forward voltage is exceeded. If you need a refresher on the junction itself, read our guide on how semiconductors work before you pick up the meter.

Do You Know?

Fluke explains in its ABCs of DMMs application note that diode test mode measures and displays the actual voltage drop across a junction. That is why the reading is in volts, not ohms.

Advertisement

How to Test a Diode with a Digital Multimeter Step by Step

Start with diode mode when you learn how to test a diode, since Fluke calls it the best method in almost every case. The meter pushes a small constant current through the junction and shows the voltage it develops.

1
Make it safe
Turn off all power and discharge any capacitors first.
2
Select diode mode
Turn the switch to the diode symbol, pressing select if it shares the continuity position.
3
Forward bias
Place the red probe on the anode and the black probe on the cathode. Record the reading in volts.
4
Reverse bias
Swap the probes so red touches the cathode. A good diode shows OL, meaning over limit or open.
5
Compare
Compare both readings with the table below or a known good diode.

You follow the same discipline as when you test a capacitor with a multimeter, because both checks need a dead circuit and discharged storage parts. Skipping the power off step is the most common cause of a burnt fuse or a strange reading.

Quick Tip

Hold the diode body, not the metal leads, while you test. Your fingers across both leads add a parallel path that can make an open reverse reading look leaky.

What Reading Should a Good Diode Show?

A good diode shows a forward drop that matches its family and OL in reverse. The table below lists typical diode mode readings at the small test current of a handheld meter.

Diode typeTypical forward readingReverse readingNote
Silicon rectifier (1N4007)0.5 to 0.8 VOLMost common reading on the bench
Schottky (1N5819)0.15 to 0.45 VOL or highHigher leakage is normal
Germanium (OA91)0.2 to 0.3 VOL or highFound in older radios
Red LED1.6 to 2.0 VOLMay glow faintly in diode mode
Blue or white LED2.6 to 3.2 VOLMeter may show OL if test voltage is low
Zener (any voltage)0.6 to 0.8 VOLZener voltage needs a supply test

Schottky parts read low because the metal to semiconductor barrier is smaller, as our article on Schottky diode advantages and limitations explains. Do not reject a Schottky just because it reads 0.3 V, because that is normal for this type.

LEDs need a higher forward voltage because of their wide band gap materials, which is covered in our LED working principle tutorial. A blue or white LED may stay dark and read OL on a meter whose open circuit test voltage is below about 3 V.

Do You Know?

Datasheets quote forward voltage at much higher current than a meter uses. The 1N4007 datasheet lists a maximum of 1.1 V at 1 A, while a multimeter at around 1 mA usually shows nearer 0.6 V.

Advertisement

How Do You Know If a Diode Is Bad?

A diode is bad when both readings look the same, either OL both ways or a low value both ways. Fluke notes that an open diode shows OL in both directions and a shorted diode reads about 0.4 V in both directions.

Good

Forward reading within the expected range and OL with the probes reversed.

Best for: Keep in service
PASS
Open

OL in both directions because the junction or a bond wire has failed.

Best for: Replace the diode
OPEN
Shorted

Near zero or the same low value in both directions.

Best for: Replace and find the cause
SHORT
Leaky

Normal forward reading but a value instead of OL in reverse.

Best for: Confirm out of circuit
LEAKY

A shorted rectifier diode usually points to a surge or overload. Our article on diode rectifier circuits shows where each diode sits and which faults stress it.

Myth: If the forward reading looks fine, the diode is good.
Fact: You must also check reverse bias, because a shorted or leaky diode can still show a normal looking forward drop.
Myth: Diode mode can tell you the voltage of any Zener diode.
Fact: Most meters test at about 2 to 3 V, so a 5.1 V or 12 V Zener simply reads OL in reverse and needs a supply test.
Myth: A diode that tests good on the bench will work at full load.
Fact: A meter tests at about 1 mA, so high current faults can pass.

Can You Test a Diode with Resistance Mode?

Yes, you can use resistance mode when your meter has no diode function, but the result is only a rough good or bad check. Fluke says a forward biased good diode reads roughly 1 kilohm to 10 megohm and shows OL in reverse.

Diode mode
  • Shows the real forward voltage in volts
  • Easy to compare with a readings table
  • Separates silicon, Schottky and LED types
  • Often beeps on a shorted junction
Resistance mode
  • Reading changes with the selected range
  • Some low ranges cannot forward bias the junction
  • Cannot identify the diode family
  • Useful only to confirm a fault already found

The ohms reading depends on the test voltage and current, so it does not obey a simple Ohm's law calculation like a resistor would. Two good diodes of the same type can show quite different resistance values on different ranges.

Quick Tip

On an old analog multimeter the black lead is often the positive terminal in ohms mode. Check your meter manual before you decide which end is the anode.

How to Check a Diode in Circuit Without Removing It

You can check a diode in circuit for a quick screen, but any reading that looks wrong must be confirmed with one leg lifted. Fluke warns that testing diodes in a circuit can give false readings because other parts sit in parallel.

In circuit symptomLikely causeWhat to do
Low reading both waysParallel resistor or transformer windingLift one diode leg and retest
Forward reading lower than tableAnother junction in parallelCompare with the circuit diagram
Beep on a bridge diodeShorted diode or shorted loadIsolate the bridge from the load

A relay coil with a flyback diode is a classic case where the coil winding hides the diode. Our relay coil suppression guide shows why the coil reads only a few hundred ohms across the diode.

Testing Zener Diodes, LEDs and Bridge Rectifiers

Special diodes need one extra step beyond the basic forward and reverse check. A Zener needs a reverse breakdown test, an LED needs enough test voltage to light, and a bridge needs each of its four diodes tested.

ZenerDiode mode shows a normal forward drop. For the Zener voltage, feed it in reverse through a series resistor and measure across it.
LEDUse diode mode and watch for a faint glow. If the meter reads OL, use a 5 V supply and a series resistor instead.
BridgeTest from each AC pin to the plus and minus pins in both directions. Four forward readings and four OL readings mean the bridge is healthy.

The Zener supply test is explained in our article on what a Zener diode is, and the series resistor is sized just like an LED resistor. You can size it quickly with the LED resistor calculator and then use the calculator below to check current.

For a deeper look at the diode itself, this beginner diode explainer covers symbols, packages and basic circuits. Our diode types guide lists where each family is used in industrial boards.

Diode Forward Current and Vf Check Calculator

Enter the supply, the series resistor and your measured drop, and the calculator gives the forward current and grades the reading. Use it when you practise how to test a diode with a bench supply.

Diode Series Resistor Current and Vf Check
Result
I = 24.04 mA, diode power 16.8 mW, resistor power 272 mW, Vf 0.70 V is normal silicon range

The solved example below uses the same default numbers as the calculator, so you can follow every line by hand. It also shows why a quarter watt resistor is too small here.

I = (Vs minus Vf) ÷ R
I = (12 minus 0.7) ÷ 470
I = 11.3 ÷ 470 = 24.04 mA
Diode power = 0.7 × 24.04 = 16.8 mW
Resistor power = 11.3 × 0.02404 = 272 mW

The resistor dissipates 272 mW, which is above a 0.25 W rating, so pick a 0.5 W part for this test. A 0.7 V drop at 24 mA confirms a normal silicon junction, and the same formula helps when you study transistor junctions which behave like two diodes.

Field Tips for Diode Testing in Panels and Boards

Most field mistakes come from rushed probing, live circuits and missing comparisons. Run through this checklist before you condemn a diode on a control panel or a power supply board.

  • Isolate supply and confirm zero volts with the meter before probing
  • Discharge filter capacitors through a suitable resistor
  • Select diode mode, not continuity alone
  • Record forward and reverse readings, not just one
  • Lift one leg if any reading looks doubtful

How to Test a Diode FAQ

What reading should a good diode show on a digital multimeter?

A good silicon diode shows about 0.5 to 0.8 V forward and OL in reverse in diode mode. Germanium reads lower at roughly 0.2 to 0.3 V.

If both directions show the same value, the diode is faulty, so confirm it out of circuit and then replace it.

What is the difference between diode mode and resistance mode for testing?

Diode mode shows the forward voltage drop in volts, while resistance mode shows ohms that change with the selected range. Diode mode is preferred because readings compare directly with a table.

Resistance mode is only a backup for meters without the diode function, where a good diode reads high forward and open in reverse.

How do you know if a diode is open, shorted or leaky?

An open diode reads OL both ways, and a shorted diode reads near zero or about 0.4 V both ways. A leaky diode shows a normal forward drop but a value instead of OL in reverse.

Always confirm a suspected leaky part with one leg lifted from the board.

How to test a diode in circuit without removing it from the board?

You can screen a diode in circuit, but parallel resistors, windings and other junctions can give false low readings. Switch power off and discharge capacitors first.

If a reading looks wrong, lift one leg and test again, because only an isolated diode gives a reliable result.

Why does a Schottky diode read lower than a normal silicon diode?

A Schottky diode uses a metal to semiconductor junction with a lower barrier, so it typically reads 0.15 to 0.45 V in diode mode. That low reading is normal and does not mean the part is shorted.

Schottky parts also have higher reverse leakage, especially when warm, so a high but finite reverse reading is acceptable.

How do you test a 12 V Zener diode with a multimeter step by step?

First check it in diode mode, where a good Zener reads about 0.7 V forward and OL reverse. A meter cannot reach 12 V, so it cannot show breakdown.

Next feed it in reverse from a 15 V supply through a 470 ohm resistor and measure across the Zener, which should read close to 12 V.

Which common mistake gives false readings when testing a diode?

The most common mistake is testing with power still applied or with charged capacitors on the board. Another is holding both metal leads with your fingers, which adds a parallel path.

Weak meter batteries also lower the test voltage and can make LEDs read OL, so replace the battery when readings look odd.

What We Learn Today

  • Knowing how to test a diode means checking forward and reverse readings in diode mode, where a good silicon part shows about 0.6 V and OL.
  • Open diodes read OL both ways, shorted diodes read low both ways, and leaky diodes show a reading in reverse instead of a clean OL.
  • In circuit readings can mislead because of parallel parts, so lift one leg and use a supply test for Zener voltage and bright LEDs.
